sections.title: Speech That Builds Up the Assembly

blocks.text: Paul describes tongues as prayer or praise directed to God, mysterious to hearers, meaningful enough to be interpreted, and capable of edifying the speaker. Those descriptions do not settle exactly what every Corinthian utterance sounded like. His immediate test is whether gathered worship becomes understandable and beneficial: without interpretation, the speaker is to keep silent in the assembly, while spirit and understanding belong together.

Prophecy is preferred in the gathering because it addresses people for upbuilding, encouragement, and consolation. It is not thereby placed beyond scrutiny: two or three may speak, others weigh what is said, and one speaker yields when another receives a revelation. Spiritual intensity or a claimed revelation therefore does not cancel shared discernment, self-control, or the aim of peace.

The Isaiah citation and the claim that tongues are a sign are followed by contrasting visitor scenes. Uninterpreted speech can make outsiders conclude that the church is mad, while intelligible prophecy can disclose the heart and direct a visitor toward God. The later instructions regulate numbers, sequence, interpretation, and turn-taking so that many may contribute without confusion. Order serves intelligibility, participation, and peace rather than spectacle or suppression.

Verses 34-35 occur in all extant Greek witnesses, although some Western witnesses place them after verse 40. Within this chapter, silence is also required of an uninterpreted tongue speaker and of a prophet when another receives a revelation. That repeated pattern makes both effortless deletion and a universal rule rendering women permanently voiceless too simple. The precise activity, audience, and scope of these verses remain disputed.

sections.title: Love and the Wider Gift Discussion

blocks.text: Chapter 13 stands between the discussions of gifts in chapters 12 and 14. In that setting, love corrects rivalry, self-display, and competitive knowledge rather than functioning chiefly as an isolated reflection on romance. Its patience, kindness, delight in truth, and refusal to insist on its own way show why communal worship cannot be separated from truthful and noncoercive treatment of others.

At Pentecost in Acts, an international crowd recognizes languages or dialects. That scene illuminates the importance of intelligible communication, but the available material does not make it an exact definition of every phenomenon at Corinth. The relationship between these early Christian accounts of speech remains debated.

Paul's appeal to order cannot be detached from his repeated purposes: people are to learn, receive encouragement, understand what is said, and participate in peace. It therefore cannot justify monopolized speech, coerced public display, disability exclusion, retaliation against questions, or the silencing of safeguarding concerns. Practices claiming spiritual authority remain subject to intelligibility, communal evaluation, and care for those who enter the gathering.
